newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin heads for G7 summit buoyed by tax victory.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin heads for G7 summit buoyed by tax victory.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday headed for the Group of Seven industrialised nations' summit in the United States buoyed by news that Russia's parliament had backed his government's draft tax code.

Before flying to Denver for the three-day gathering that starts on Friday, Yeltsin hailed the State Duma's tentative approval of the tax code as a "huge victory" that would help put Russia on the path to economic recovery.
"This is a huge victory for us...This is also a big move for foreign businessmen," Yeltsin said.
He said lower taxes should help lure more foreign investors to his country, which still suffers from an image of heavy-handed bureucracy, rampant corruption and uncertain rules.

Yeltsin, who was speaking to reporters from the G7 countries in an interview later carried by Russia's commercial NTV channel, said the Denver summit would have a broad scope including arms control, social problems and regional conflicts.
Russia is keen to be admitted as a full-fledged member of the G-7, which includes the United States, Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan.

"Such a decision would be a historic one for Russia," said Yeltsin, who has attended five previous G7 summits and has taken part in their political discussions. This year he will also participate in talks on selected economic issues and will be excluded only from a one-hour session on financial matters.
However Yeltsin said he would not be attending the July summit of NATO states in Madrid.

The Madrid summit is awkward for Moscow because it is expected to take a decision on inviting some east European countries to join, a move Russia, which signed a cooperation deal with NATO in May, sees as damaging its security interests.
In Thursday's interview Yeltsin expressed concern over the big gulf that has opened up in post-communist Russia between the haves and have-nots.
"Half of our people, if not more, are for the time being living in poverty...Now all our work is aimed at restoring social justice," he said.

The Duma lower house of parliament, which is dominated by Yeltsin's communist opponents, has been under heavy pressure from ministers to approve the tax code as well as a range of spending cuts aimed at putting Russia's finances in order.

On Tuesday the Duma threw out a package of bills to reduce or scrap most Soviet-era welfare benefits, which the cabinet says have become too heavy a burden for the new Russia. The cuts would mostly affect the poor and elderly -- the main electorate of the opposition.

On Wednesday, the Duma again stalled a government plan to cut spending in the 1997 budget, but the government has said the cuts will go ahead irrespective of the vote. The Duma will consider its own budget-cutting plan on Friday.

Ministers say the draft tax code discussed by parliament on Thursday is crucial to future budgets, helping to cut domestic producers' tax burden, stabilise the tax system and decrease tax pressure on private individuals.

In the Duma, 254 deputies backed a resolution passing the code in the first reading. Only 84 voted against. The resolution contains several clauses designed to help the Duma save face and says the second reading of the bill should start on November 1.
The draft suggests cutting the number of tax groups of Russian citizens and businesses to 28 from 75.
As a result the government will lose 73-75 trillion roubles ($12.6-$13 billion), but enterprises would save money and be able to make greater investment, ministers say.

Private individuals will pay a 30 percent income tax on annual earnings of more than 60 million roubles and only 12 percent on anything below that level. Russia is currently using a five-grade tax system with a top rate of 35 percent.
